title: The Spider's Web
subtitle: Open it, reread it. Witness firsthand the events that transpired within the desert.

trails.title: Typewriter Record #P12
trails.description: They cover their eyes. They descend into madness.

content.text:
When they speak of "Manus Vindictae," their tone is always light, often laced with jokes—colorful descriptions like "a greasy-headed musician smearing tiles like a drunk Edward Goya" frequently crop up in their poetry. Even though I have never "seen" such a scene myself, I can still grasp their attitude toward Manus Vindictae—it was an oppression surpassing even their past sufferings. Yet, subconsciously, they "ignored" this similarity—perhaps out of denial, or perhaps because this prison had already taught them to obey, also subconsciously.

But as far as I know, Manus Vindictae did bring their terror here. Those masks drove arcanists to insanity and caused unbearable suffering, as if they were caught in an inescapable snare. After prolonged torment, they lost the ability to utter even a single phrase of their own language, reduced to slaves of this underground faction—left with only a singular thought, their souls having left the empty husk of their former selves.

And as for humans—it seems they were driven to death en masse. At night, they were not allowed prolonged sleep, woken by their companions every hour to sit beneath the watchtower and chant prayers. And by dawn, high-intensity training and interrogations that did not require or expect any answers would begin again ... The purpose of Manus Vindictae is buried beneath these cruel methods, as clear as the deepest crevasse in the ice field—it is nothing but destruction. They seek to "completely destroy" humanity.

items.text: The Spider's Web

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Ladies, I must apologize for what happened back there.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: We were caught off guard. There has never been a commotion of that scale before. I must report this to the Physician.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Don't worry, Ms. Jailer. We made it out in one piece.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Thank you for your understanding. Ordinarily, I would arrange to escort you to a safer location, but I'm afraid at this hour, you'll have missed the last train. And the roads are icy at night.
Hearing this, Recoleta exchanges a quick but meaningful expression with her companions.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Psst, Vertin. We can't leave like this.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: We appreciate your kind consideration, Ms. Jailer, but we still have some unfinished business here.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I see. I'll arrange a clean room in a safer section for you.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: We'll do our best to ensure your safety tonight.
Cell, Comala Prison
Night falls as the girls huddle together, scrutinizing their unfamiliar surroundings.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: They actually found us a spare room.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Bleak, quiet, and somber. It's a cell like all the others.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Don't worry. This isn't the first time we've ended up on the wrong side of the bars.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: At least this time we're just here for the night, not a full sentence.
Sonetto lets out a whisper-thin protest.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Though, this cell is quite different from the ones we've been in before.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Not just this cell. The whole prison is unlike anything I've seen.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: And this society they've been running here isn't some mere pastime. They're having real discussions about meaningful topics, even though the rest of the world has been cut off from them.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: But we're still in an arcanist prison, a place where conflicts and violence can erupt at any moment. Let's not forget that.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Ms. Jailer warned us from the start. These prisoners are mentally unstable and potentially dangerous.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Ms. Recoleta, with all due respect, we can't afford to see this place through rose-colored glasses. We'd be overlooking the risks, as we did earlier.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: And with all due respect, Sonetto, we didn't overlook any danger. At least I didn't. A writer must be observant if she is to accurately reflect the world in her writing.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: But you—

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: We came here with different goals, and still, none of them have been accomplished.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: I suggest we focus on our respective missions instead of fighting with one another.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Apologies, Timekeeper. Ms. Recoleta, I take back everything I said.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Don't apologize, Sonetto. I'm at fault, too. Sometimes I forget that words can be as sharp as swords. You were only thinking about our safety. I shouldn't have been so rude.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I actually really admire how you fought back there! If you'd allow me, I'd like to write a poem for you, once my novel's finished.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Ah ...

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: That's terribly kind of you. But honestly, I think we've had enough poetry today to last a lifetime.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Let me know if you change your mind. By the way, did either of you see what happened to the Idealist?
Recalling their recent conflict, the indomitable girl finally hesitates.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: The jailer told me she went back to the gallery once everything calmed down.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: She found nothing: no blood, no shell cases, not even a trace of the Idealist.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Timekeeper, now's really not the time for ghost stories.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Do you mean that maybe the Idealist somehow managed to get out of there on his own?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Or perhaps someone else helped him.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Well, according to the Idealist and our jailer, any inmates who are unwell will be taken to the Physician.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: It's possible someone brought him there while everyone else was shouting and running about.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: You're right. It could be that he's with the Physician right now. I'm relieved! That was a sudden plot twist, but a visionary of his magnitude doesn't deserve to die in silence like that.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: To be fair, the gunshot was quite loud, as was the ensuing commotion.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Nonetheless, he couldn't have just died like that! I mean, the readers would riot if a writer were to kill off a character so abruptly!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But, you believe he's still alive, too. Am I right?
She knows her words are merely a cover. She needs an answer—a real, undeniable answer.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: There's nothing that we can be certain of for now. But on a brighter note, we didn't come back empty-handed from our mission either, Sonetto.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: We found Dr. Dores's signature in the gallery. You were right all along, Recoleta. She was here.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: But we didn't see her at the gathering. Could something have happened to her, like with the Idealist?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Do you think she was also sent to the Physician and never made it back?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: This is all just speculation. If we want to find the Idealist or Dr. Dores ...

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: We need to speak to this Physician first.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Ms. Recoleta, do you believe that the Idealist could be your pen pal, Aleph?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Whether he is or not, he's still my best lead.
That name touches a nerve once again.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Friends, I've had this strange feeling in my gut since we got here. Something is slowing us down.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Now to figure out what it is ...
A silent fear grips her, like ripples suddenly appearing on a once-still lake, unsettling in its quiet disturbance.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Look, it's a wild guess, but just wait till I finish.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: It feels like everything happening in this prison is somehow connected to my novel, The Rise and Fall of Sanity.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: We're no strangers to wild guesses, and sometimes they're closer to the truth than you'd think. So this ...

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: The Rise and Fall of Sanity.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Sorry. What exactly is your story about?
The question scatters the midnight gloom. Outside, moonlight spills over gray-white snow.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Hah! I never thought that you'd be interested!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: It starts—sorry, it's been a while since I told it from the beginning: A few, a few years ago, I worked, worked as a forest ranger. It happened in a desert town called Amalfitano, in Sonora back in 1975 ...
Two patient listeners watch the stammering girl, waiting for the next part of her story.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Ah, you know what? Most people say the beginning's a bit hard to get into, except for Aleph. I'm thinking of rewriting it.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But if you like the sound of it so far, maybe I could read you the latest part I just finished?
She studies her readers' expressions, guessing madly at their responses.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Please.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: "It all started with the frequency data from the tapes."

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: "The general pattern seemed to have changed. At first, the Paracausality Researcher chalked it up to a statistical error—a glitch, perhaps."—Oh, sorry.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But after a few days and long nights of meticulous calculations, that explanation only became less and less plausible. The odds of success and failure kept shifting, and the chance of repeating the previous result kept growing. It was as if someone had tampered with the rules and tweaked it to their liking.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: She took her findings to Amalfitano, "the town of nothing," as they called it then.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Near the old looms, she met a blind weaver who spoke softly of an old tale:

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: "I heard a strange rustling at dawn, like a die rolling along a wooden floor. Then the morning light dimmed and died. That was the last time I saw the sun, my own hands, or the threads I worked with."

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: "The second time I heard the die roll, I was told the oxen in the field sank to their knees and never stood again."

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: "By the third roll, the fields were crawling with frogs. Plows ran over them, and some still writhed, squeezing themselves deeper into the cracks in the earth."

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: "The fourth time the die rolled, ten dormice plunged into the sea in a strange sleepwalk, and ten bears feasted for the last time before winter arrived."

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: "The final roll of the die was cast in a cage, during a duel, before a crowd of eager eyes. The winner left with ten pounds of gold, and the loser left with ten flies which fell on him to feast."
The quiet spreads through their cell like a rolling tide.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Is that all?

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Emm. Seems like it.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Well, there's more, but I haven't quite figured those parts out yet.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Any thoughts? Anything? I can take it. Please. I really need some feedback.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: I ... I wonder if the protagonist ever finds this "Die of Babylon" in the end.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Oh, Vertin, it isn't a real die. It's just a metaphor!

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Oh, I see. I must've missed that. Sorry. Still, it's a beautiful story. Sad, but beautiful.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: The story is still too obscure, isn't it? *sigh* Aleph warned me about this. In our last correspondence, he suggested adding the Blind Weaver to shed light on the hidden theme.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: It helped at first. But even with this sage advice, no matter how hard I tried, the plot just didn't seem to move forward.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I feel stuck in that village with them—lost, dazed, isolated inside their small, disconnected moments. Something crucial is missing, leaving gaps between the characters and scenes.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Should I change the storyteller's perspective? Start a different angle? Or maybe rewrite the characters completely? What should I do?
Before the writer sinks into a swirling vortex of self-doubt, someone decides to push for something tangible.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Apologies, but you said your story somehow connects to what's happening here in the Panopticon. What makes you think that?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: It's a strange feeling. Like everything here belongs to a dream I once had, only I can't remember it.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Do you mean that you have a sense of déjà vu?

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: It's nothing to worry about. Our psychiatrist friend, Kakania, told me those moments are often the result of a dysfunctional connection between two parts of the brain, like a little glitch in our heads.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: No, it's nothing like déjà vu!
The storyteller snaps back, politely agitated.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Déjà vu is a single moment, a specific situation. But here it's everything! La Sociedad, the rules, the Idealist, even the incidents in the gallery! Each one unfolds in a similar pattern, like the grooves on a record, telling a story I feel I've listened to before.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Amalfitano and Comala. They're two sides of that same record, playing out the same tune. Whatever happens in my story seems to be happening here too.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I had that feeling when I met you as well, Ms. Vertin.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: At first, I thought it was only an interesting coincidence. You're much like the first character in my story—a traveler with a suitcase.
The girl rambles on, desperately relating to her characters.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But then I realized, the doctor, your Dores—she's like the Blind Weaver, who lost her sight to the die despite having always been faithful to it.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: And the jailer—she's the Bank Clerk who assisted the corporation in taking over the town in order to escape her past.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: And the Idealist? He's the Murdered Donkey Driver. And the Die of Babylon ... No ...

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: My dear fictional friends ... What on earth is happening to you?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Wait. Are you saying that everyone we've met here matches a character from your story, like some kind of archetype?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: That sounds unbelievable. But, then again, maybe you're onto something.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: You see the world through a different lens that none of us share.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Not just the characters! The events here are mirroring my story, too.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Aleph—he's the only one who truly understood my story. If things are playing out just like my novel, then ...

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Maybe Aleph is in fact still here.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Are you suggesting that someone is controlling the Panopticon in order to make it follow the same plot as your story?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: That they've set the rules, started the poetry group, planned the attack on the Idealist, and tried to prevent us from finding Dr. Dores?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: If that's true, Ms. Recoleta, it's very likely that the one acting against us is in fact Aleph himself.
Recoleta never expected the chain of reasoning to unravel this way.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But I ... No ... How could that be possible?!
She interrupts, only for confusion to creep onto her face moments later.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Why? Why would he do this?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I don't see any reason why he'd be connected. He's an intelligent, cultured, and profound person, not a common killer.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: No, none of this adds up.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Remember, Dr. Dores was brought to Ushuaia by the Zeno rebels.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: And we know they're connected to Manus Vindictae.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: If this Aleph really is hiding Dores from us, he may be working with them.
Recoleta stares blankly for a time before clumsily shifting the topic.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Oh my, Sonetto! I didn't know you had such a flair for stories! Maybe you should join us and become a visceral realist too.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I think you're only imagining things. Perhaps you were inspired by this strange prison? Haha.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Perhaps we all need to start writing our own stories.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Come out, now. Whoever's out there, speak up.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: How can we help you?

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Who's there?
